card.title: Electromotive force (emf), internal resistance, and cells…

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Emf is the open-circuit voltage of a source. Internal resistance drops the terminal voltage to E − I r while the cell supplies current, and the loop current is E/(R+r). Identical cells in series add their emfs. Identical cells in parallel keep one emf and share the internal resistance.

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
V = IR
P = IV = I²R = V²/R
V_term = E − Ir

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ state the rule without its limit → ✅ note when it applies / stops applying.  ·  ❌ no diagram → ✅ add one labelled figure / structured list.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: On open circuit, I = 0 and V = E.  ·  Charging a cell reverses the current, and the terminal voltage becomes E + I r.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: The emf of a cell is the work done per unit charge as charge is moved through the source. It is measured in volts. It is the open-circuit potential difference, when no current is drawn.  ·  A real cell has internal resistance r. When current I flows, the terminal voltage is E − I r. The 'lost volts' I r heat the inside of the cell.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: electromotive force, internal resistance, cells in combination (within Current Electricity).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Physics — don't mix them.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Emf  ·  Internal resistance  ·  Terminal voltage  ·  Series and parallel cells

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Emf is the energy per unit charge from the source.  ·  Internal resistance is inside the cell.  ·  Terminal voltage is less than emf when the cell supplies current.  ·  Series cells add emfs. Parallel equal cells share current.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Ohm's law: V = IR; R = ρL/A (resistivity ρ depends on material).  ·  Series: R = ΣR; same I, voltages add. Parallel: 1/R = Σ1/R; same V, currents add.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: What is the emf of two identical cells in parallel?

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: A cell of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω is connected to a 2.5 Ω resistor. Find the current and the terminal voltage.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: On open circuit the terminal voltage equals → B  ·  While supplying current, V equals → A

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: The current in a single loop is I = E / (R + r). A smaller external resistance draws a larger current and drops the terminal voltage further. Shorting a cell makes I = E/r, which can be large and damaging.  ·  Two identical cells in series give emf 2E and internal resistance 2r, if they point the same way. The current in an external R is 2E / (R + 2r).  ·  Two identical cells in parallel give emf E and internal resistance r/2. The parallel pair can supply a larger current before the terminal voltage sags, but the emf is still the emf of one cell.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ skip the key fact → ✅ ohm's law: v = ir; r = ρl/a (resistivity ρ depends on material)..  ·  Emf is not the terminal voltage under load.  ·  Lost volts are I r, not I R.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Parallel identical cells do not double the emf.  ·  A short circuit is I = E/r, not zero.  ·  Say whether the cell is supplying or being charged before using the sign of I r.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Do not add emfs of a parallel pair.  ·  Write I = E / (R + r) and say what each symbol means.  ·  Mark the known values, then substitute one step at a time.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Finish with the number, the unit, and the direction when the quantity has one.  ·  Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R; internal resistance makes terminal V = E − Ir.  ·  State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Limit to remember: ohm's law: v = ir; r = ρl/a (resistivity ρ depends on material).  ·  Cells in opposition subtract their emfs. A 1.5 V cell set against a 1.5 V cell gives no net emf if they are identical, and a small difference of emf drives a current limited by both internal resistances.  ·  # Electromotive force (emf), internal resistance, and cells in combination ## 1.
